name: Question 5
problem: Let $f(x,y)$ be a function that is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where $a=⟨-3,-1⟩$ and $b=⟨-1,-2⟩$ are the position vectors of $A$ and $B,$ respectively. If $f(a)=-1$ and $f(b)=3,$ then according to the mean value theorem, which of the following must be true for some point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c?$
worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(b)-f(a) & =∇f(c)·(b-a) \\ 3-(-1) & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c)⟩\cdot (⟨-1,-2⟩-⟨-3,-1⟩) \\ 4 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c)⟩\cdot ⟨2,-1⟩ \\ 4 & =2{f}_{x}(c)-{f}_{y}(c).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Let f(x,y) be a function that is differentiable at each point on the line segment AB―, where a=⟨−3,−1⟩ and b=⟨−1,−2⟩ are the position vectors of A and B, respectively. If f(a)=−1 and f(b)=3, then according to the mean value theorem, which of the following must be true for some point C∈AB― with position vector c?

a
−2fx(c)+fy(c)=4
b
−4fx(c)−3fy(c)=4
c
2fx(c)−fy(c)=4
d
fx(c)−2fy(c)=−4
e
−2fx(c)−3fy(c)=−4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The mean value theorem states that if f(x,y) is differentiable at each point on the line segment AB―, then there exists a point C∈AB― with position vector c such that

f(b)−f(a)=∇f(c)·(b−a).

In our case, we have f(b)−f(a)=∇f(c)·(b−a)3−(−1)=⟨fx(c),fy(c)⟩⋅(⟨−1,−2⟩−⟨−3,−1⟩)4=⟨fx(c),fy(c)⟩⋅⟨2,−1⟩4=2fx(c)−fy(c).
